content: Norethindrone is prescribed to treat endometriosis, a condition where the tissue that normally lines the uterus grows in other parts of the body, causing pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and other symptoms. It is also used to treat abnormal menstrual bleeding or to restore a normal menstrual cycle in women who previously menstruated regularly but have not had a period for at least six months, provided they are not pregnant or undergoing menopause. Additionally, norethindrone is used as a diagnostic tool to determine if the body is producing certain female hormones that affect the uterus. Norethindrone belongs to a class of medications called progestins. It works by preventing the uterine lining from growing and by stimulating the uterus to produce specific hormones. It is also used in smaller doses to prevent pregnancy, though this monograph does not include information on its contraceptive use. For details on that, refer to the monograph titled Progestin Only Oral Contraceptives. Norethindrone is available as an oral tablet and is taken on different schedules depending on the condition being treated and its effectiveness. For endometriosis, it is typically taken once daily for 6 to 9 months or until breakthrough bleeding becomes problematic. To induce a normal menstrual cycle in women who have stopped menstruating, it is usually taken once daily for 5 to 10 days during the second half of the planned menstrual cycle. To ensure consistent use, take norethindrone at the same time each day as directed. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not take more or less of the medication or take it more frequently than prescribed. If you are taking norethindrone for endometriosis, your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it, no more than once every two weeks. While norethindrone can help manage your condition, it does not cure it. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking norethindrone, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to norethindrone, oral contraceptives, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention medications for seizures (e.g., carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin) and rifampin, as your doctor may need to adjust your doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have recently had surgery, been immobile for any reason, or have a history of breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, missed abortion, blood clots, stroke, coronary artery disease, chest pain, heart attack, thrombophilia, seizures, migraines, depression, asthma, high cholesterol, diabetes, or heart, kidney, or liver disease. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking norethindrone, contact your doctor immediately. Norethindrone should never be used to test for pregnancy. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking norethindrone. Additionally, let your doctor know if you smoke, as smoking may increase the risk of serious side effects associated with norethindrone. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Norethindrone may cause side effects. Mild side effects include irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting, changes in menstrual flow, breast tenderness or enlargement, upset stomach, weight changes, difficulty sleeping, acne, or facial hair growth. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include vision loss, blurred or double vision, bulging eyes, migraines, pain or heaviness in the lower leg, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, sudden chest pain, difficulty speaking, dizziness, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, swelling of extremities, yellowing of the skin or eyes, depression, mood swings, brown patches on the face, missed periods, severe abdominal pain, hives, rash, itching, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. If you experience any unusual problems while taking norethindrone, contact your doctor. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store norethindrone in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as they may order tests to monitor your response to norethindrone. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking this medication before undergoing any tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
